# On the Strange Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking about boredom lately—how we treat it like a disease rather than a messenger.

We're terrified of it. The moment a waiting room appears or a commute stretches before us, we reach for our phones like they're oxygen masks. We've engineered boredom almost entirely out of modern life, replacing empty moments with infinite content. And yet something feels lost in the transaction.

Boredom, I think, is where the mind does its best work. Not the focused, productive work we celebrate—the kind with metrics and deliverables. But the wandering kind. The kind where your mind connects seemingly unrelated ideas, where you finally understand why you've been irritable all week, where a forgotten dream resurfaces.

The best ideas I've had arrived during tedious tasks. Walking somewhere. Washing dishes. Staring out a window. There's something about the brain when it's neither stimulated nor sleeping, when it's left to its own devices. That's where the real thinking happens.

I'm not romanticizing mindlessness. But I think we've overcorrected. We've become so afraid of stillness that we've forgotten it's the soil where creativity grows.

Next time you're bored, maybe resist the reflex. Sit with it a moment. Notice what surfaces when you're not drowning it out. You might find that boredom isn't emptiness at all—it's the space where your own thoughts finally have room to breathe.

That's worth something.
